Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Do not perform the task.", "input": "please turn this into a clear prompt for preparing a technician work order and the related resident communication for an intercom repair at maple house. i have details in different places, so arrange them without making the repair decision for us. this is a four-floor, 18-unit apartment building, and the intercom is an older system, probably installed in the late 1980s. The lobby panel is beside the main entrance, the electric strike is on that door, and the master controller is in a locked utility cabinet in the basement. The cabinet key is held by building manager Imani Cole, who can meet the technician. caretaker Leo Grant first logged a problem on May 6, after a resident called him around 7:40 in the morning. Since then there have been separate reports, not one confirmed description of a single fault. Please keep that distinction clear.

Mara in 2C said, “I can hear the lobby, but nobody hears me.” That was her report on May 6. Joel from 4A called on May 7 and said, “The button clicks, but the door stays shut.” He was talking about his handset door-release button, not the lobby call button. Don't convert that into a conclusion that the controller is faulty or that a reset fixed anything. Imani says the original installation booklet has not been found. Leo has a folded page with a hand-drawn list of apartment numbers, but he isn't sure it's current, so don't present it as a verified wiring map.

What we need is a practical work order for a technician to inspect and troubleshoot the reported issues, rather than a diagnosis written in advance. Ask the technician to record which symptom can be reproduced, where, and under what test conditions, and to separate audio findings from door-release findings. Include a place to note the date and time, the technician's name, the equipment or connections inspected, tests performed, results, and any limits on the inspection. The technician should check the lobby panel and the electric strike as part of the investigation, and inspect the basement controller only with Imani providing access. Don't tell the technician to open apartment handsets or enter occupied units automatically; arrange each unit check with the resident first. We can ask residents whether they will be available, but no unit access has been promised.

For a first comparison, Imani suggested asking about handsets in 1A, 2C, 3B, and 4A. Those are suggested sample units, not a complete survey and not proof that the others work or fail. Mara is in 2C and Joel is in 4A; we don't yet have permission or a time for either apartment visit. The technician should note which units were actually tested, whether someone answered at the lobby panel, whether two-way conversation worked, and whether the release button operated the strike. If a sample unit can't be accessed, record that as not tested instead of filling in a result. Don't label something defective just because no one answers or because a resident is unavailable. If more tests are needed beyond the initial checks, have the technician describe what further access or information is needed rather than assuming it can be obtained that day.

Please include this decision condition clearly in the work order: if the strike releases during a lobby test but any handset tested still has one-way audio, don't describe the intercom as fully restored. Record the door-release and audio results separately and leave the audio issue open for further investigation. Conversely, if audio works in a particular test but the strike does not release, report those findings separately too. These are reporting instructions; they don't tell us what the cause is or authorize a repair. No replacement parts or paid work beyond inspection and troubleshooting have been approved. If the technician believes a part needs replacement or proposes work that would add cost, ask for an estimate and the reason before any such work is authorized. Do not word the work order as if approval has already been given.

The visit is being coordinated for June 12, between 9 a.m. and noon, but the technician has not confirmed that window. Phrase it as a proposed or requested visit window, not a confirmed appointment. Imani can meet at the building and open the basement cabinet during that period if the visit goes ahead. Leo can point out the lobby panel and share the earlier log entry, but he isn't authorized to approve extra work. Make the work order useful if the time changes, and don't promise residents that a technician will definitely arrive then.

Please also draft a short resident update to go with the work order. It should say that reports have been received about intercom audio and door release, that inspection is being arranged, and that residents may be contacted to coordinate access to selected apartments. Don't say that the intercom is out for everyone, that it has been repaired, or that a particular apartment will definitely be visited. Ask residents who have a problem to report their unit number, when it happened, whether they could hear and be heard, and whether the door opened after pressing the release button. Keep the update calm and factual; don't include personal contact details beyond naming Imani Cole as the building manager and Leo Grant as the caretaker.

Use a numbered section in the prompt for the required work-order contents: (1) reported symptoms and their sources, (2) access and equipment checks, (3) test results recorded separately for audio and the strike, (4) estimates or further access needed, and (5) a clear status field that does not call the system restored if the condition above applies. Then request the separate resident update. Keep the quoted remarks and the earlier visit note exactly as written, because those are the source wording we have. The result should be an organized request that someone can use to prepare these two documents; it should not itself supply a diagnosis, fill in test results, approve spending, confirm the visit, or claim that any repair has happened. Be specific about the uncertainty and access limits, but don't add a new repair procedure or a building-wide conclusion that isn't in these notes.", "output": "Prepare a technician work order and a separate resident update for the reported intercom problems at Maple House. Use the information below to organize the request without supplying a diagnosis, test results, spending approval, confirmed appointment, or claim that a repair has happened. Keep reported observations distinct from verified findings and do not assume that all reports have one cause.

## Building and coordination details

Maple House is a four-floor, 18-unit apartment building with an older intercom system, probably installed in the late 1980s. The lobby panel is beside the main entrance; the electric strike is on that door; and the master controller is in a locked utility cabinet in the basement. Building manager Imani Cole holds the cabinet key and can meet the technician. Caretaker Leo Grant first logged a problem on May 6, after a resident contacted him at about 7:40 a.m.

A visit is being coordinated for June 12, between 9 a.m. and noon, but the technician has not confirmed that window. Describe it as a proposed or requested window, not a confirmed appointment. Imani can meet the technician and open the basement cabinet during that period if the visit goes ahead. Leo can point out the lobby panel and share the earlier log entry, but he cannot approve extra work. Do not promise residents that the technician will arrive at that time, and make the work order useful if the time changes.

## Reports and source notes

Keep the reports separate; they do not confirm that every handset or the whole building is affected, or that the reported problems have one cause.

- On May 6, Mara in 2C said, “I can hear the lobby, but nobody hears me.”
- On May 7, Joel in 4A said, “The button clicks, but the door stays shut.” He meant his handset door-release button, not the lobby call button.
- On May 8, a first-floor resident told Leo that the sound had been faint. Leo did not record the unit number or whether the problem involved incoming or outgoing audio. Do not assign the report to a particular apartment.
- Some people mentioned rain the night before the May 6 report. There is no evidence that rain caused anything; mention it only if relevant, and do not present it as a cause.

The date and author of an earlier visit note are unknown. Keep it as a note, not a confirmed repair record: “Power cycled at 9:20; fault returned before lunch.” There is no record of which component was power cycled, what test was performed, or how the reported return of the fault was established. Do not conclude that the controller is faulty or that a reset fixed anything. Imani says the original installation booklet has not been found. Leo has a folded page with a hand-drawn list of apartment numbers, but he is unsure it is current; do not present it as a verified wiring map.

## Work order request

Ask the technician to inspect and troubleshoot the reported issues rather than work from a diagnosis written in advance. The work order should provide space to record the date and time, technician’s name, equipment or connections inspected, tests performed, results, and any limits on the inspection. Ask the technician to record which symptoms can be reproduced, where they occur, and under what test conditions. Require audio findings and door-release findings to be recorded separately.

Include checks of the lobby panel and electric strike. The basement controller should be inspected only with Imani providing access. Do not direct the technician to open apartment handsets or enter occupied units automatically; arrange each unit check with the resident first. Residents may be asked whether they are available, but no unit access has been promised.

For an initial comparison, Imani suggested handsets in 1A, 2C, 3B, and 4A. These are suggested sample units, not a complete survey and not evidence that other units work or fail. Mara is in 2C and Joel is in 4A; neither permission nor a time for a visit to either apartment has been confirmed. Ask the technician to note which units were actually tested, whether someone answered at the lobby panel, whether two-way conversation worked, and whether the release button operated the strike. If a unit cannot be accessed, record it as not tested. Do not label equipment defective because nobody answers or a resident is unavailable. If further tests are needed beyond the initial checks, have the technician identify the access or information needed rather than assume it will be available that day.

Include this reporting condition: if the strike releases during a lobby test but any handset tested still has one-way audio, do not describe the intercom as fully restored. Record the audio and door-release results separately and leave the audio issue open for further investigation. Likewise, if audio works in a particular test but the strike does not release, report those findings separately. These are reporting instructions only; they do not establish a cause or authorize a repair.

No replacement parts or paid work beyond inspection and troubleshooting have been approved. If the technician believes a part needs replacement or proposes work that would add cost, request an estimate and the reason before any such work is authorized. Do not word the work order as if approval has already been given.

Include these numbered work-order contents:
1. Reported symptoms and their sources.
2. Access and equipment checks.
3. Test results recorded separately for audio and the strike.
4. Estimates or further access needed.
5. A clear status field that does not call the system restored if the reporting condition above applies.

## Resident update

Draft a short, separate update saying that reports have been received about intercom audio and door release, inspection is being arranged, and residents may be contacted to coordinate access to selected apartments. Do not say the intercom is out for everyone, has been repaired, or that a particular apartment will definitely be visited. Ask residents experiencing a problem to report their unit number, when it happened, whether they could hear and be heard, and whether the door opened after they pressed the release button. Keep the message calm and factual. Do not include personal contact details beyond naming Imani Cole as the building manager and Leo Grant as the caretaker.

Keep the quoted remarks and earlier visit note exactly as written. The requested output is an organized prompt for preparing the work order and resident update, not the documents themselves. Preserve the uncertainty about the reports, the limits on access, and the proposed timing; do not add a repair procedure, a building-wide conclusion, or any other facts not provided here."}]
